column1: # Profile routes: the names both languages agree on and what `bench run`
# starts for each wrapped request. Read by the Rust tests (runner.rs) and the
# Tab-separated. '#' starts a comment line. A '-' field is empty. In a route,
# <dir> is the folder the wrap writes into (<output-dir>/<binary>.<canonical
# tool>), <cwd> the working directory and <whole-dir> the folder named whole,
# <cwd>/<dir>, each with every '%' doubled, and <bin> the benchmark;
# arguments are separated by single spaces. compute-sanitizer joins a
# relative log name to its working directory before it reads '%' macros,
# so its log is named whole.
# escape   <--profile>  <--profile-args>  <--profile-output-dir>  <output option>  <its value in the route>
# (valgrind's output options, compute-sanitizer's --log-file and the -o of
# nsys and ncu read a '%' in the value as the start of a macro such as %p,
# and %% as one '%': each '%' of the folder is doubled, and the output lands
# in the folder as named. heaptrack's -o replaces %h and %p and has no
# escape: any other '%' reaches it as it is, and a folder holding %h or %p is
# refused, in the refuse-folder rows below)
# unwrapped   <--profile>  (the benchmark runs itself; --profile-args reach it untouched)
